examShortTricks: Trick 1: Unit-theme questions ask you to CONNECT the text to Nepali context — always end an answer with one sentence applying the theme to Nepal (heritage tourism, cultural preservation).
Trick 2: For 'history and culture' passages, watch for dates, dynasties and customs in comprehension questions — underline them while reading; most factual questions quote them directly.
Trick 3: Critical writing questions on culture usually ask agree/disagree — use the PEEL frame (Point, Example, Explain, Link) and one counter-argument for the top band.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why should a society preserve its cultural heritage? Give two reasons in your own words. (2 marks) — identity and continuity; economic value through tourism.
Q. How does understanding history help us understand the present? (2 marks) — present institutions and conflicts have historical roots; history explains current values.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Theme questions on love/relationships expect BALANCE — present both the emotional and the practical side of the relationship in the text before giving your view.
Trick 2: Character questions: describe the character with ONE quoted action or line from the text, then interpret — quotation + interpretation is the full-mark pattern.
Trick 3: In inference questions, never answer with a fact stated in the text; the mark is for what the text IMPLIES.
practiceQuestions: Q. What does the text suggest about the nature of true love? (2 marks) — care and sacrifice beyond attraction; support the point with one event from the text.
Q. Justify the title of the story you have studied in this unit. (2 marks) — link the title's literal and symbolic meanings with one plot event.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Health passages are data-heavy — circle numbers and comparatives (more, less, twice) while reading; comprehension questions target them.
Trick 2: Essay questions on exercise expect a structured argument: claim → two benefits with reasons → one counter-view (no time) → rebuttal → conclusion.
Trick 3: Use the text's own vocabulary (cardiovascular, immunity, sedentary) — examiners reward topic-specific lexis over generic words.
practiceQuestions: Q. Give two benefits of regular exercise mentioned in the text. (2 marks) — stronger heart/immunity and better mental health (adapt to the text's list).
Q. Why do young people exercise less today? Suggest two reasons. (2 marks) — screen time and busy schedules; add one solution.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Development-vs-environment questions need a BALANCED stance — acknowledge development's need, then argue for sustainability; one-sided answers lose the top band.
Trick 2: Cause–effect signal words (because, as a result, consequently) mark the relationships comprehension questions test — track them.
Trick 3: For letter-to-the-editor answers on environment, follow: salutation → problem with one local example → two effects → two solutions → sign-off.
practiceQuestions: Q. How can a country develop without destroying nature? Suggest two ways. (2 marks) — renewable energy and eco-tourism (or strict EIA and recycling).
Q. Why are forests important for a country like Nepal? (2 marks) — biodiversity, water regulation and soil protection; tourism income.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Distinguish the pair for the definition mark: humour amuses; satire CRITICISES through amusement — every unit question rewards naming the satire's TARGET.
Trick 2: Identify the devices: irony, exaggeration (hyperbole), parody, sarcasm — name the device AND the sentence that shows it.
Trick 3: When asked 'what is the writer satirising?', answer in one sentence naming the social vice (greed, hypocrisy, bureaucracy), not the plot.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the difference between humour and satire? (2 marks) — humour entertains; satire exposes and criticises folly through humour.
Q. Name two satirical devices with an example from the text. (2 marks) — irony/hyperbole with the quoted line.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Rights questions expect the three generations in order: civil-political (vote, speech), socio-economic (education, health), collective (development, environment) — structure the answer this way.
Trick 2: Link rights to responsibilities in one sentence — 'every right implies a duty' — it lifts an average answer to the top band.
Trick 3: Use Nepal-specific anchors: 2072 constitution, inclusive representation, local elections — concrete examples beat abstractions.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why are human rights called universal? (2 marks) — they belong to every person regardless of status and are not granted by any state.
Q. What duties accompany the right to education? (1 mark) — attend and learn; respect teachers and school property.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Family-theme answers score by CONTRAST — joint vs nuclear, tradition vs modernity; present both sides before your stance.
Trick 2: For 'describe your family' style free writing, use one vivid specific detail per member instead of general praise — specific detail is the top-band marker.
Trick 3: Inference questions about relationships: watch dialogue and what characters DO, not what the narrator says.
practiceQuestions: Q. What are two advantages of a joint family? (2 marks) — shared support and care of elders/children; lower living cost.
Q. How have family roles changed in modern life? (2 marks) — shared earning, smaller households, technology-mediated contact.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Art questions want the FUNCTION named: expression, communication, preservation of culture, therapy — pick two and argue, not a list.
Trick 2: When analysing a picture/poem in this unit, move from what you SEE to what it MEANS — observation then interpretation is the marking ladder.
Trick 3: 'Should art be censored?' type questions: state the principle (freedom of expression) then the limit (harm to others) — balanced principle-based answers win.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is art important in society? Give two reasons. (2 marks) — expresses identity and preserves culture; provokes thought and change.
Q. Should all art be free from censorship? (2 marks) — defend expression, but accept limits where art incites harm.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Fantasy questions test SUSPENSION OF DISBELIEF — explain how the writer makes impossible events feel real (consistent rules, vivid detail, relatable characters).
Trick 2: Symbol questions: fantasy objects usually symbolise real desires or fears — name the symbol and its real-world meaning.
Trick 3: 'Why do readers enjoy fantasy?' — answer with escapism PLUS insight: fantasy tells truths about reality through the impossible.
practiceQuestions: Q. What makes a fantasy story believable? (2 marks) — internal consistency of the imagined world and characters with real emotions.
Q. What might a magical object in the story symbolise? (2 marks) — a real human wish or fear; justify from the plot.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: CV/cover-letter questions follow fixed formats — memorise the CV sections (personal details, objective, education, experience, skills, references) and the letter's block layout; format errors cost the most marks.
Trick 2: Job-application questions reward SPECIFICITY — name the post, the source of the vacancy, and match two of your skills to the job requirements.
Trick 3: Entrepreneurship questions: define (self-employment creating value) → two qualities (risk-taking, innovation) → one Nepali example.
practiceQuestions: Q. List any four sections of a CV in order. (2 marks) — personal details, objective, education, experience (plus skills/references).
Q. Give two qualities of a successful entrepreneur. (2 marks) — risk-taking and creativity/persistence, with one line each.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Politics passages use loaded language — separate FACT from OPINION; comprehension questions ask you to identify the writer's stance, so track evaluative words.
Trick 2: 'Power corrupts' essay: define → one historical example → one modern example → safeguard (accountability, free press) — structure beats rhetoric.
Trick 3: In debate-style answers, pre-empt the opposition: 'Some argue... however...' — acknowledging the other side is the top-band move.
practiceQuestions: Q. How can power be kept in check? Suggest two ways. (2 marks) — independent judiciary/media; periodic free elections.
Q. Why do people abuse power? (2 marks) — lack of accountability and human greed; give one example.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: War texts test TONE — identify whether the writer condemns, mourns or glorifies; tone questions ask for evidence (word choice, imagery), not just a label.
Trick 2: Anti-war answers score with COSTS in three columns: human, economic, psychological — one line each beats a paragraph of emotion.
Trick 3: For 'is war ever justified?' — use the just-war frame: self-defence and last resort; then argue diplomacy first.
practiceQuestions: Q. What are the costs of war to ordinary people? (2 marks) — death, displacement and trauma; economic destruction.
Q. How can peace be promoted among nations? (2 marks) — diplomacy and international organisations; trade and cultural exchange.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Identify the fallacy bank: hasty generalisation, ad hominem, false cause, appeal to emotion — naming the flaw in an argument is the unit's core skill.
Trick 2: Evaluate claims with the CARS test: Claim, Assumptions, Reasons/evidence, Standard of proof — a quick scaffold for 'do you agree?' questions.
Trick 3: Distinguish fact (verifiable) from opinion (judgement) — quote one sentence of each from the passage to secure the marks.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the difference between a fact and an opinion? (1 mark) — a fact can be verified; an opinion expresses belief or judgement.
Q. Identify one weakness in the writer's argument. (2 marks) — name the fallacy (e.g. hasty generalisation) and quote the offending line.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Globalisation answers need BOTH faces: opportunity (trade, technology, jobs) and threat (cultural erosion, inequality) — one-sided answers sit in the middle band.
Trick 2: Diaspora questions revolve around identity — 'neither fully here nor there'; use the words displacement, nostalgia, hybrid identity.
Trick 3: Bring the answer home: remittance economy and brain drain are Nepal's two lived dimensions of this theme.
practiceQuestions: Q. Give two effects of globalisation on local culture. (2 marks) — spread of global media erodes local language/dress; but also revives interest through global audiences.
Q. What challenges do diaspora communities face? (2 marks) — identity conflict and discrimination; loss of language across generations.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Error-spotting ladder: subject–verb agreement → tense consistency → article use → preposition → word form — check in this fixed order and you stop missing items.
Trick 2: Agreement traps: collective nouns (singular in AmE), 'each/every/either' take singular; 'a number of' plural, 'the number of' singular — memorise the four traps.
Trick 3: For transformation questions, identify the STRUCTURE being tested (too...to → so...that; as soon as → no sooner...than) — transformations are pattern swaps, not rewrites.
practiceQuestions: Q. Correct: 'Each of the boys have a pen.' (1 mark) — Each ... has (each takes a singular verb).
Q. Transform: 'As soon as he saw the police, he ran away.' (1 mark) — No sooner had he seen the police than he ran away.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Word-formation questions: prefix/suffix changes part of speech — 'happy (adj) → happiness (noun) → happily (adv)'; identify the base word first.
Trick 2: Context-clue method for unseen vocabulary: definition, example, contrast (but/however), and cause signals around the unknown word give the meaning without a dictionary.
Trick 3: Synonym questions: check the word's PART OF SPEECH in the sentence first — a synonym must match both meaning AND word class.
practiceQuestions: Q. Give the noun form of 'strong' and the adjective form of 'beauty'. (1 mark) — strength; beautiful.
Q. Find a word in the passage meaning 'very large'. (1 mark) — locate the adjective near a size context (e.g. enormous).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Dialogue completion: match TONE and FORMALITY to the situation — an apology needs 'I'm sorry... I'll...'; a request needs 'Could you... please?' — register is the hidden mark.
Trick 2: Telephone/announcement conventions: identify yourself first, state purpose second, confirm details third — the three-move structure.
Trick 3: For role-play questions, keep each turn SHORT and move the conversation forward with a question — examiners reward interaction, not monologue.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a polite request to borrow a friend's notes. (1 mark) — 'Could you please lend me your notes? I'll return them tomorrow.'
Q. Complete a telephone conversation asking for an appointment. (2 marks) — identify yourself, state the purpose, propose a time, confirm.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Theme in one line: divine justice and forgiveness outweigh human law — Ivan's pardon of Makar is the proof event; quote it.

Trick 2: Irony is the device to name: the title promises God sees the truth but WAITS — 26 years of suffering before truth emerges; explain the double irony (Makar confesses, Aksyonov dies before release).
Trick 3: Character change question: track Aksyonov from carefree merchant to spiritual, resigned prisoner — pick two contrasting moments (early suspicion of wife; final forgiveness).
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the significance of the title? (2 marks) — God knows the truth but his justice comes in his own time; Aksyonov's 26-year wait shows this.
Q. How does Aksyonov change in Siberia? (2 marks) — from a worldly, quick-tempered merchant to a saintly, forgiving man.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The entire story is a CHILD'S IMAGINATION on a carpet — say this first; the 'snakes' and 'lava' exist only in the boy's mind.
Trick 2: Suspense technique: short sentences, present-tense immediacy, ticking-clock pressure (mother calling) — name two techniques with examples.
Trick 3: The ambiguous ending (did he step on red?) is deliberate — discuss what the open ending suggests about imagination and fear.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the boy pretending as he crosses the carpet? (1 mark) — that red patches are red-hot coals and black ones snakes.
Q. Why does the story end ambiguously? (2 marks) — to leave the reader inside the child's suspense; the game's danger is imaginary yet felt as real.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Central message: resilience after war — Jonathan's refrain 'Nothing puzzles God!' shows gratitude and adaptability; quote the refrain.
Trick 2: The bicycle, the house, the egg-rasher money: each represents survival's stages — structure a theme answer around these three symbols.
Trick 3: The thieves' episode is treated with dark humour, not despair — explain how Achebe's tone celebrates endurance rather than mourning loss.
practiceQuestions: Q. What does Jonathan's exclamation 'Nothing puzzles God' reveal about him? (2 marks) — resilient faith and gratitude; he counts blessings even after loss.
Q. How does the family survive after the war? (2 marks) — bicycle taxi service, repaired house, Jonathan's job and the egg-rasher.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Theme: loneliness of soldiers and innocent rivalry in love — both friends love the same woman silently; the tragic irony is that neither 'wins'.
Trick 2: Setting does the work: the Paris barracks vs the countryside walks — contrast the settings to explain the soldiers' longing for warmth.
Trick 3: The ending's irony: the woman was married all along — the soldiers' rivalry was pointless; name this dramatic irony explicitly.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why do the two soldiers visit the countryside? (1 mark) — to escape barracks loneliness and enjoy the company of the kind countrywoman.
Q. What is ironic about the ending? (2 marks) — both men's silent rivalry was unnecessary: the woman was already married.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The astrologer's power is KNOWLEDGE, not the stars — he knows Guru Nayak because he left him for dead years ago; this twist is the whole story.
Trick 2: Irony and fate: the man he 'killed' survived and searched for him — the astrologer is both the criminal and the comforter; state the double role.
Trick 3: Atmosphere questions: the twilight crowd, the flare, the market — sensory detail hides his ordinary trickery; link setting to theme of deception.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does the astrologer know so much about Guru Nayak? (2 marks) — he was the village youth who stabbed him and left him for dead.
Q. Why does the astrologer feel relieved at the end? (2 marks) — the man he thought he murdered is alive; his lifelong guilt lifts.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The poem personifies CORONAVIRUS as a speaker defending itself — the reversal (virus accusing humans) is the poem's central irony; state it first.
Trick 2: The virus's argument: humans destroyed nature and each other; the pandemic only balanced the scales — collect two lines supporting this accusation.
Trick 3: Message questions: humility before nature and reflection during lockdown — connect one image (empty roads, clear skies) to the message.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does the speaker (corona) claim humans deserved the pandemic? (2 marks) — humans exploited nature and waged wars; corona presents itself as nature's correction.
Q. What positive changes does the poem note during lockdown? (2 marks) — cleaner air, family time, reflection on priorities.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The four similes are the poem — rose (beauty), melody (sweetness), the seas drying (eternity), the flower of June (youth); each simile = one mark in analysis.
Trick 2: Hyperbole question: 'till a' the seas gang dry' and 'rocks melt wi' the sun' are deliberate exaggerations of eternal love — name the device and its effect.
Trick 3: Dialect note: 'bonnie', 'gang', 'wi'' — Scots dialect adds intimacy and folk-song quality; mention it for the style mark.
practiceQuestions: Q. What two things does the speaker compare his love to? (2 marks) — a red rose and a sweet melody.
Q. Why does the speaker use exaggeration? (1 mark) — to express the boundless, eternal nature of his love.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The extended metaphor: life = drama, people = actors, God = playwright — state the controlling metaphor before anything else.
Trick 2: The seven ages in order: infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (old man), second childhood — memorise the list; sequencing questions are guaranteed.
Trick 3: The last age is the harshest: sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything — the repetition 'sans' drives the message of decline; quote it.
practiceQuestions: Q. List the seven ages of man. (3 marks) — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, second childhood.
Q. What is the message of the poem? (2 marks) — life is a predictable performance from entry to exit; humans merely play their parts.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The speaker watches a small child ('little i') watching the sunset — the poem is about wonder and the adult's lost ability to see freshly; state this reversal.
Trick 2: Cummings's typography: lowercase 'i', broken syntax, compressed lines — the form itself enacts childlike simplicity; name the style.
Trick 3: November sunset imagery: 'gold red' sky, 'the quivering leaf' — connect one image to the mood of quiet wonder.
practiceQuestions: Q. Who is 'little i' and what is he doing? (2 marks) — a small child gazing at the November sunset from a window.
Q. Why does Cummings write 'i' in lowercase? (1 mark) — to humble the ego and mirror the child's smallness and wonder.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Structure: each stanza pairs a GIFT the speaker offers with the war's grim 'gift' returned — the ironic exchange is the poem's device; explain one pair.
Trick 2: Anti-war message through personal loss: flowers and youth exchanged for a grave and death — the contrast between tender gifts and war's returns is the theme.
Trick 3: The address to the dead beloved (apostrophe) makes grief intimate — name the device and its emotional effect.
practiceQuestions: Q. What 'gifts' does war return to the speaker? (2 marks) — her beloved's grave, the smell of death, a lost youth — war's cruel exchanges.
Q. What is the tone of the poem? (1 mark) — mournful and bitterly ironic.
